record.cfhi_compre_01_bench_paragraph___days_of:
This ratio tells how many days of operating expenses are available in net asset reserves. Net asset reserves take into account the accrual of current assets and current liabilities. The term expendable net assets represents the total resources available to spend on operations, excluding future gifts made or revenues generated by the church. Think of it as how long you could live on a savings account. Expendable net assets consist of net assets without donor restrictions, undesignated (formerly referred to as unrestricted, undesignated net assets), which are net assets that result from achieving positive net income year after year in the without donor restrictions column of the statement of activities. It also includes reserves designated by the board for specific operating purposes, but excludes reserves that represent the church's equity in land, buildings, and equipment (NIFA).


The total of the amounts in the numerator is divided by total expenditures less the annual non-cash expense of depreciation. The net result of removing depreciation is to calculate, based on prior expenditures, the cash expenses your church would incur. The number of days can be temporarily high if the church has recorded large gifts without donor restrictions that have not been spent at year-end. This is the case for churches with fiscal years ending on December 31, when many attendees give large year-end gifts in order to meet tax-reporting deadlines. The number of days can also appear low if the church incurred a large one-time expenditure that won't be repeated in the future. This result indicates that the church has an amount within or above the recommended benchmark.
record.cfhi_compre_02_bench_paragraph___days_op:
This ratio calculates the days of operating cash and investments on hand to fund annual cash expenditures, but specifically related to very liquid assets. It only considers operating cash and investments, not other current assets and liabilities. This number is divided by the sum of expenses plus capitalized interest, which is interest paid in cash but not expensed by the church. This may occur during periods of construction when GAAP requires the church to capitalize this cash expense as part of the cost of the asset being built. Depreciation is also removed because it represents a significant non-cash annual expense recorded by the church. Current debt principal is added back because it represents cash spent, but it is not recorded as an expense in the financial statements. The net effect of these adjustments is to estimate, based on prior expenditures, the annual cash expenditures the church would incur.


This result indicates that the church has an amount within or above the recommended benchmark. These reserves can be used for economic downturns or unexpected expenses, events, or new opportunities. Often, churches that try to build up reserves have a goal. If a goal has not been set, we recommend setting and maintaining one.
record.cfhi_compre_04_bench_paragraph___liquidi: This ratio will tell the reader how many times actual operating liabilities can be funded from operating reserves. These operating liabilities exclude current building fund liabilities, which normally have a separate source of cash from restricted revenues or budgets. It also excludes any amounts owed on a short-term construction line of credit. These are typically interest-only until converted into a long-term debt and paid over time, and do not require payment from operating cash or investments in the short-term. It also excludes deferred revenues, which do not require an outlay of cash. This result indicates that the church has an amount within or above the recommended benchmark.
record.cfhi_compre_05_bench_paragraph___net_cas:
This measurement calculates the amount of cash available for other uses after the church has satisfied its adjusted current liabilities (excluding amounts borrowed on a construction line of credit) and cash and investments set aside for projects with donor restrictions (excluding non-cash amounts or pledges receivable from donor-restricted projects) resulting from gifts given by donors who have placed restrictions on their use.


This may be one of the most important measures provided to your church leadership. Many churches today find that senior management (pastoral staff) and the governing board want to know how much cash the church has. The most important question is not "How much do we have?" but rather, "Whose cash is it and how much of it can we spend?" Those are typically two very different answers.


A net cash availability number factors in the cash required for the immediate future (less than 10 days) to determine what can safely be spent. Net assets with donor restrictions are not to be expended for general operating purposes and therefore are excluded from the cash balance. Keep in mind that the portion of net assets with donor restrictions that are supported by pledges receivable are excluded (deducted from total net assets with donor restrictions) as they would have no impact on this cash-based calculation. Some churches have in essence "borrowed" from reserves with donor restrictions because they overspent in operations. This calculation will help management identify if this is happening in your church, so it is crucial to provide this information to decision makers. This result indicates that the church has an amount within or above the recommended benchmark.
record.cfhi_compre_06_bench_paragraph___debt_to:
This ratio measures how many times debt is greater than annual contributions without donor restrictions, which are the primary income source for most churches. Lenders look at debt as funded by contributions without donor restrictions because those are the resources from which the church will be able to pay mandatory debt service payments. By looking at trends in various congregations, contributions without donor restrictions help the lender determine what debt load the church will be able to handle on top of other required expenditures (salaries, benefits, mission expenses, facility expenses, etc.). Based on our experience with church clients across the country, we realize the lower this ratio is, the less strain debt will be on the church's budget.


This result indicates that the church has an amount within or above the recommended benchmark and is easily able to handle the level of debt it is presently carrying.
record.cfhi_compre_07_bench_paragraph___current:
This ratio helps determine how easily the church can meet its current obligations through current assets. There are differences of opinion as to what the ratio results should be. A ratio of less than 1.0 could be interpreted as a red flag that the church does not have enough in current assets to pay its upcoming liabilities. This could result in the need to borrow from restricted funds or the need to obtain a temporary line of credit to cover short-term obligations. Results this low would also warrant a careful review of the cash flow and reserves ratios and measurements. Your church will need to be aware of this and monitor the ratio on an ongoing basis to avoid being surprised by a cash shortage.


This result indicates that the church has an amount within or above the recommended benchmark, and is easily able to handle the level of current liabilities it is presently carrying and still have reserves remaining.
record.cfhi_compre_08_bench_paragraph__mandator: This ratio pertains more to the debt service (debt payment requirements), and looks at the percentage of contributions that will be used to make annual debt service payments. Although a church may have many revenue sources, lenders typically only consider contributions without donor restrictions when determining how much debt a church can manage. This result indicates that the church has an amount within or above the recommended benchmark and is easily able to handle the level of debt service it is presently carrying.
record.cfhi_compre_09d_bench_paragraph___debt_p: This figure is calculated by dividing total debt by the average number of giving units. It will vary significantly based on the philosophy, denomination, location, age, size, and demographics of the church. Each church will need to determine the level of debt it is comfortable maintaining or servicing. You will probably encounter varying opinions within your congregation. Some individuals believe that a church should not incur debt while others are very comfortable with a high debt load. Lenders believe that debt will be funded by contributions without donor restrictions because typically these are the resources from which the church will be able to pay mandatory debt service payments. This result indicates that the church has a level of debt per giving unit within or below the recommended benchmark and is easily able to handle the level of debt it is presently carrying.
record.cfhi_compre_10_bench_paragraph___debt_co:
This ratio is used to determine how many times a church would be able to cover its current annual debt obligations from current operations. This is a very common debt covenant ratio used by lenders to monitor the ability of a church to make annual debt service payments. The results could change dramatically between years based on swings in the change in net assets without donor restrictions. For example, if a church used its reserves to perform more repairs and maintenance to its facility than normal, the increase in expense could cause a much lower positive or even negative change in net assets without donor restrictions. This would adversely affect the ratio and could unexpectedly violate a debt covenant, potentially requiring the church to obtain a bank covenant waiver and pay related fees. The benchmark agreed to by the lender is a key negotiation point, especially with a new lender. It may also factor into the amount of reserves the church leadership deems necessary.


The change in net assets without donor restrictions is primarily driven by operational decisions such as successes or failures at managing budgeted expenses. Successes or failures at developing good stewardship habits in the congregation, resulting in growth or decline of contributions without donor restrictions, can also have a significant effect on this number. Interest expense represents interest payments under the terms of the note. The biggest factor impacting this ratio is significant increases or decreases to the change in net assets without donor restrictions . Ministry decisions or necessary additional expenditures may drive the decision to spend net assets without donor restrictions and result in lower positive or negative change in net assets without donor restrictions. While a lower positive or negative change in net assets without donor restrictions may impact this ratio in the current year, it is important to look at the trends and understand the reasons behind ministry decisions to spend resources without donor restrictions. This result indicates that the church has an amount within or above the recommended benchmark and is able to cover its current annual debt obligations from current operations.
record.cfhi_compre_11_bench_paragraph___net_inc:
The purpose of this ratio is to show if the results of the church's general operations are positive or negative, and by how much. In business terms, this shows if the church is making or losing money in its basic day-to-day function of ministering to the local community. The importance of this ratio is immediately apparent. If a church is losing money in its basic operations over time, eventually it will no longer be viable and will have to close. At some point this church will reach the stage where it is either too late to make the necessary operational changes or it no longer has the funds or the confidence to make them. That point is more easily identified in retrospect, but the net income ratio can provide a bellwether to warn of impending financial distress.


One factor to consider when calculating this ratio is that very large one-time events, such as the receipt of a large one-time gift without donor restrictions made at the end of the fiscal year, can significantly influence a church's net operating income. Your church may not want to have large surpluses every year. You may want to make sure that money is invested in the ministries of the church. However, you need to make sure some reserves are in place. Monitoring this ratio and the trend of it from year to year will help determine the financial health of your church. This result indicates that the church has a negative net income trend, which places it in the action required range. There are many ministry reasons why a church may or may not choose to show consistent surpluses. It is because of these reasons that the ratio is also calculated using the average net income over several years, to determine if recent deficits are a one-time issue or a growing, unchecked trend. Because your average trend is negative, it is necessary to immediately identify the reasons behind this trend and how to quickly change it. Urgently taking steps to increase net operating income will have the single most positive impact on it.
record.cfhi_compre_13v19b_bench_paragraph___tot: Have you ever wondered what the net position (per average adult attendee and giving unit) is between the total contributions received (excluding accrual pledges and large one-time gifts) and the financial cost per adult attendee and giving unit? This comparison takes the net between these two measures and gives you the information to know if your contributions are high enough to cover the cash cost per adult attendee and giving unit. Because the net position of these two measures is positive, the result is within the recommended limits and your church can conclude that you are able to fund cash operations though current contributions received.
record.cfhi_compre_14_bench_paragraph___median_: The purpose of this ratio is to see what percentage of the local median county household income adult attendees and giving units are contributing to your church. The median income figure is obtained from the most recent U.S. Census data available, which is usually one year in arrears. Your church must be aware of the demographics of your congregation as compared to the county's demographics if you are in a large county with much economic diversity. This ratio allows your church to see the percentage of median household income your adult attendees and giving units contribute to your church. Trends between years in this data are very important. This percentage and the changes between years allow management and the board to see how much additional giving capacity the congregation has. It also is great feedback for the senior pastor to see changes in giving habits between years and in response to stewardship teaching and focus. This result indicates that the church has an amount within or above the recommended benchmark.
record.cfhi_compre_17_1_bench_paragraph___perso:
Salaries and benefits represent significant resource outflows from the local church. Therefore, it is essential to continually monitor these levels as a percentage of cash expenditures. It is also important to promptly follow up on changes in trends or unusual variances from peers to ensure that your ministry resources are continually maximized. This measure allows your church to look at one of its largest expenses and determine the portion of the operating budget that will be used.

This result indicates that personnel to total cash expenditures (excluding depreciation but including current debt principal) are just below the recommended limits. The best way to improve this measure is to decrease other expenses, consider the need to add employees to meet current ministry demands, or perform a compensation study to assess whether current salaries and benefits are in line with peers.
record.cfhi_compre_17_2_bench_paragraph___manda:
Interest and debt service payments (which are not an expense but rather a reduction of a liability) can represent major resource outflows from the local church. Therefore, it is essential to continually monitor these levels as a percentage of cash expenditures. It is also important to promptly follow up on changes in trends or unusual variances from peers to ensure that your ministry resources are continually maximized.

This ratio allows your church to look at two of its largest outflows and determine the portion of the operating budget that will be used. Often a growth cycle results in an amount of debt the church anticipates being able to pay off as more people are able and encouraged to attend. However, the church needs to be able to pay the bills and provide the services that will attract new people with the current budget. Reviewing this measure in advance of any major debt decisions will help you analyze the feasibility of any facility expansion goals.

This result indicates that the measure is within the recommended benchmark, and mandatory debt service payments to total cash expenditures (excluding depreciation but including current debt principal) are within the recommended limits.

If a goal has not been set, we recommend setting and maintaining one.
record.cfhi_stand_02_bench_paragraph___net_cash: This measurement calculates the amount of cash available for other uses after the church has satisfied its current liabilities and set aside funds donors have restricted for specific uses. This may be one of the most important measures provided to your church leadership. Many churches today find that senior management (pastoral staff) and the governing board want to know how much cash the church has. The most important question is not 'How much do we have?' but rather, 'Whose cash is it and how much of it can we spend?' Those are typically two very different answers. A net cash availability number factors in the cash required for the immediate future (less than 10 days) to determine what can safely be spent. This result indicates that the church has an amount within or above the recommended benchmark.
record.cfhi_stand_06and08_bench_paragraph_total:
Have you ever wondered what the net position is (per giving unit) when compared to the financial cost of total contributions received? This calculation takes the net between these two measures and gives you the information to know if your contributions are high enough to cover the monetary cost per giving unit.

Because the net position of these two measures is positive, the result is within the recommended limits and your church can conclude that you are able to pay cash operations though current contributions received.

record.cfhi_compre_01_bench_paragraph___days_of:
This ratio tells how many days of operating expenses are available in net asset reserves. Net asset reserves take into account the accrual of current assets and current liabilities. The term expendable net assets represents the total resources available to spend on operations, excluding future gifts made or revenues generated by the church. Think of it as how long you could live on a savings account. Expendable net assets consist of net assets without donor restrictions, undesignated (formerly referred to as unrestricted, undesignated net assets), which are net assets that result from achieving positive net income year after year in the without donor restrictions column of the statement of activities. It also includes reserves designated by the board for specific operating purposes, but excludes reserves that represent the church's equity in land, buildings, and equipment (NIFA).


The total of the amounts in the numerator is divided by total expenditures less the annual non-cash expense of depreciation. The net result of removing depreciation is to calculate, based on prior expenditures, the cash expenses your church would incur. The number of days can be temporarily high if the church has recorded large gifts without donor restrictions that have not been spent at year-end. This is the case for churches with fiscal years ending on December 31, when many attendees give large year-end gifts in order to meet tax-reporting deadlines. The number of days can also appear low if the church incurred a large one-time expenditure that won't be repeated in the future. This result indicates that the church has an amount within or above the recommended benchmark.
record.cfhi_compre_02_bench_paragraph___days_op:
This ratio calculates the days of operating cash and investments on hand to fund annual cash expenditures, but specifically related to very liquid assets. It only considers operating cash and investments, not other current assets and liabilities. This number is divided by the sum of expenses plus capitalized interest, which is interest paid in cash but not expensed by the church. This may occur during periods of construction when GAAP requires the church to capitalize this cash expense as part of the cost of the asset being built. Depreciation is also removed because it represents a significant non-cash annual expense recorded by the church. Current debt principal is added back because it represents cash spent, but it is not recorded as an expense in the financial statements. The net effect of these adjustments is to estimate, based on prior expenditures, the annual cash expenditures the church would incur.


This result indicates that the church has an amount within or above the recommended benchmark. These reserves can be used for economic downturns or unexpected expenses, events, or new opportunities. Often, churches that try to build up reserves have a goal. If a goal has not been set, we recommend setting and maintaining one.
record.cfhi_compre_04_bench_paragraph___liquidi: This ratio will tell the reader how many times actual operating liabilities can be funded from operating reserves. These operating liabilities exclude current building fund liabilities, which normally have a separate source of cash from restricted revenues or budgets. It also excludes any amounts owed on a short-term construction line of credit. These are typically interest-only until converted into a long-term debt and paid over time, and do not require payment from operating cash or investments in the short-term. It also excludes deferred revenues, which do not require an outlay of cash. This result indicates that the church has an amount within or above the recommended benchmark.
record.cfhi_compre_05_bench_paragraph___net_cas:
This measurement calculates the amount of cash available for other uses after the church has satisfied its adjusted current liabilities (excluding amounts borrowed on a construction line of credit) and cash and investments set aside for projects with donor restrictions (excluding non-cash amounts or pledges receivable from donor-restricted projects) resulting from gifts given by donors who have placed restrictions on their use.


This may be one of the most important measures provided to your church leadership. Many churches today find that senior management (pastoral staff) and the governing board want to know how much cash the church has. The most important question is not "How much do we have?" but rather, "Whose cash is it and how much of it can we spend?" Those are typically two very different answers.


A net cash availability number factors in the cash required for the immediate future (less than 10 days) to determine what can safely be spent. Net assets with donor restrictions are not to be expended for general operating purposes and therefore are excluded from the cash balance. Keep in mind that the portion of net assets with donor restrictions that are supported by pledges receivable are excluded (deducted from total net assets with donor restrictions) as they would have no impact on this cash-based calculation. Some churches have in essence "borrowed" from reserves with donor restrictions because they overspent in operations. This calculation will help management identify if this is happening in your church, so it is crucial to provide this information to decision makers. This result indicates that the church has an amount within or above the recommended benchmark.
record.cfhi_compre_06_bench_paragraph___debt_to:
This ratio measures how many times debt is greater than annual contributions without donor restrictions, which are the primary income source for most churches. Lenders look at debt as funded by contributions without donor restrictions because those are the resources from which the church will be able to pay mandatory debt service payments. By looking at trends in various congregations, contributions without donor restrictions help the lender determine what debt load the church will be able to handle on top of other required expenditures (salaries, benefits, mission expenses, facility expenses, etc.). Based on our experience with church clients across the country, we realize the lower this ratio is, the less strain debt will be on the church's budget.


This result indicates that the church has an amount within or above the recommended benchmark and is easily able to handle the level of debt it is presently carrying.
record.cfhi_compre_07_bench_paragraph___current:
This ratio helps determine how easily the church can meet its current obligations through current assets. There are differences of opinion as to what the ratio results should be. A ratio of less than 1.0 could be interpreted as a red flag that the church does not have enough in current assets to pay its upcoming liabilities. This could result in the need to borrow from restricted funds or the need to obtain a temporary line of credit to cover short-term obligations. Results this low would also warrant a careful review of the cash flow and reserves ratios and measurements. Your church will need to be aware of this and monitor the ratio on an ongoing basis to avoid being surprised by a cash shortage.


This result indicates that the church has an amount within or above the recommended benchmark, and is easily able to handle the level of current liabilities it is presently carrying and still have reserves remaining.
record.cfhi_compre_08_bench_paragraph__mandator: This ratio pertains more to the debt service (debt payment requirements), and looks at the percentage of contributions that will be used to make annual debt service payments. Although a church may have many revenue sources, lenders typically only consider contributions without donor restrictions when determining how much debt a church can manage. This result indicates that the church has an amount within or above the recommended benchmark and is easily able to handle the level of debt service it is presently carrying.
record.cfhi_compre_09d_bench_paragraph___debt_p: This figure is calculated by dividing total debt by the average number of giving units. It will vary significantly based on the philosophy, denomination, location, age, size, and demographics of the church. Each church will need to determine the level of debt it is comfortable maintaining or servicing. You will probably encounter varying opinions within your congregation. Some individuals believe that a church should not incur debt while others are very comfortable with a high debt load. Lenders believe that debt will be funded by contributions without donor restrictions because typically these are the resources from which the church will be able to pay mandatory debt service payments. This result indicates that the church has a level of debt per giving unit within or below the recommended benchmark and is easily able to handle the level of debt it is presently carrying.
record.cfhi_compre_10_bench_paragraph___debt_co:
This ratio is used to determine how many times a church would be able to cover its current annual debt obligations from current operations. This is a very common debt covenant ratio used by lenders to monitor the ability of a church to make annual debt service payments. The results could change dramatically between years based on swings in the change in net assets without donor restrictions. For example, if a church used its reserves to perform more repairs and maintenance to its facility than normal, the increase in expense could cause a much lower positive or even negative change in net assets without donor restrictions. This would adversely affect the ratio and could unexpectedly violate a debt covenant, potentially requiring the church to obtain a bank covenant waiver and pay related fees. The benchmark agreed to by the lender is a key negotiation point, especially with a new lender. It may also factor into the amount of reserves the church leadership deems necessary.


The change in net assets without donor restrictions is primarily driven by operational decisions such as successes or failures at managing budgeted expenses. Successes or failures at developing good stewardship habits in the congregation, resulting in growth or decline of contributions without donor restrictions, can also have a significant effect on this number. Interest expense represents interest payments under the terms of the note. The biggest factor impacting this ratio is significant increases or decreases to the change in net assets without donor restrictions . Ministry decisions or necessary additional expenditures may drive the decision to spend net assets without donor restrictions and result in lower positive or negative change in net assets without donor restrictions. While a lower positive or negative change in net assets without donor restrictions may impact this ratio in the current year, it is important to look at the trends and understand the reasons behind ministry decisions to spend resources without donor restrictions. This result indicates that the church has an amount within or above the recommended benchmark and is able to cover its current annual debt obligations from current operations.
record.cfhi_compre_11_bench_paragraph___net_inc:
The purpose of this ratio is to show if the results of the church's general operations are positive or negative, and by how much. In business terms, this shows if the church is making or losing money in its basic day-to-day function of ministering to the local community. The importance of this ratio is immediately apparent. If a church is losing money in its basic operations over time, eventually it will no longer be viable and will have to close. At some point this church will reach the stage where it is either too late to make the necessary operational changes or it no longer has the funds or the confidence to make them. That point is more easily identified in retrospect, but the net income ratio can provide a bellwether to warn of impending financial distress.


One factor to consider when calculating this ratio is that very large one-time events, such as the receipt of a large one-time gift without donor restrictions made at the end of the fiscal year, can significantly influence a church's net operating income. Your church may not want to have large surpluses every year. You may want to make sure that money is invested in the ministries of the church. However, you need to make sure some reserves are in place. Monitoring this ratio and the trend of it from year to year will help determine the financial health of your church. This result indicates that the church has a negative net income trend, which places it in the action required range. There are many ministry reasons why a church may or may not choose to show consistent surpluses. It is because of these reasons that the ratio is also calculated using the average net income over several years, to determine if recent deficits are a one-time issue or a growing, unchecked trend. Because your average trend is negative, it is necessary to immediately identify the reasons behind this trend and how to quickly change it. Urgently taking steps to increase net operating income will have the single most positive impact on it.
record.cfhi_compre_13v19b_bench_paragraph___tot:
Have you ever wondered what the net position (per average adult attendee and giving unit) is between the contributions received (excluding accrual pledges and large one-time gifts) and the cash cost per adult attendee and giving unit? This comparison takes the net between these two measures and gives you the information to know if your contributions are high enough to cover the monetary cost per adult attendee and giving unit.

Because the net position of these two measures is negative, your church can conclude that you are presently unable to pay the cost of cash operations though current contributions received, and the present situation requires immediate action. If this continues to occur over the long term, the church will be forced to cut existing ministry and staff to be able to fund its continued existence. There are many ministry reasons why a church may or may not choose to show consistent surpluses. It is because of these reasons that the user must immediately determine if recent deficits are a one-time issue or a growing, unchecked trend. The best and fastest way to improve this net position is to decrease cash expenditures as soon as possible, since your church has more instantaneous control over cash expenditures than over the level of contributions or adult attendees and giving units.
record.cfhi_compre_14_bench_paragraph___median_: The purpose of this ratio is to see what percentage of the local median county household income adult attendees and giving units are contributing to your church. The median income figure is obtained from the most recent U.S. Census data available, which is usually one year in arrears. Your church must be aware of the demographics of your congregation as compared to the county's demographics if you are in a large county with much economic diversity. This ratio allows your church to see the percentage of median household income your adult attendees and giving units contribute to your church. Trends between years in this data are very important. This percentage and the changes between years allow management and the board to see how much additional giving capacity the congregation has. It also is great feedback for the senior pastor to see changes in giving habits between years and in response to stewardship teaching and focus. This result indicates that the church has an amount within or above the recommended benchmark.
record.cfhi_compre_17_1_bench_paragraph___perso:
Salaries and benefits represent significant resource outflows from the local church. Therefore, it is essential to continually monitor these levels as a percentage of cash expenditures. It is also important to promptly follow up on changes in trends or unusual variances from peers to ensure that your ministry resources are continually maximized. This measure allows your church to look at one of its largest expenses and determine the portion of the operating budget that will be used.

This result indicates that personnel to total cash expenditures (excluding depreciation but including current debt principal) are just below the recommended limits. The best way to improve this measure is to decrease other expenses, consider the need to add employees to meet current ministry demands, or perform a compensation study to assess whether current salaries and benefits are in line with peers.
record.cfhi_compre_17_2_bench_paragraph___manda:
Interest and debt service payments (which are not an expense but rather a reduction of a liability) can represent major resource outflows from the local church. Therefore, it is essential to continually monitor these levels as a percentage of cash expenditures. It is also important to promptly follow up on changes in trends or unusual variances from peers to ensure that your ministry resources are continually maximized.

This ratio allows your church to look at two of its largest outflows and determine the portion of the operating budget that will be used. Often a growth cycle results in an amount of debt the church anticipates being able to pay off as more people are able and encouraged to attend. However, the church needs to be able to pay the bills and provide the services that will attract new people with the current budget. Reviewing this measure in advance of any major debt decisions will help you analyze the feasibility of any facility expansion goals.

This result indicates that the measure is within the recommended benchmark, and mandatory debt service payments to total cash expenditures (excluding depreciation but including current debt principal) are within the recommended limits.
